text:
1. Plato set out two laws concerning the gods.
2. Read beside Plato's two laws, Genesis 6 becomes difficult.
3. In Genesis 6, Yahweh is grieved in his heart.
4. In Genesis 6, Yahweh resolves to destroy every living thing.
5. By Plato's standards, Yahweh in Genesis 6 is both moved and a cause of harm.
6. Plato wrote his laws against gods who do evil out of caprice.
7. The flood in Genesis has a reason.
8. The reason for the flood is that the earth is filled with violence.
9. The reason for the flood narrows the conflict with Plato's laws but does not remove it.
10. Plato allows a god to punish if the poet can show that the punishment is just.
11. Plato allows a god to punish if the poet can show that the one punished is made better by it.
12. No one is made better by a flood.
13. Plato does not allow a god to feel grief.
14. Plato rejects divine grief because being grieved means being changed.
15. For Plato, a good god cannot be affected by what is below him.
16. For Genesis, a good God is affected by what his creatures have become.
17. In Genesis, God's grief shows how seriously he takes the corruption of his creatures.
18. Noah and Socrates arrive at theology at different points in their building.
19. Noah builds under God's judgment from the beginning.
20. Noah builds the ark to dimensions given by God.
21. The God who gives Noah the dimensions has looked at the world and been wounded by it.
22. Socrates derives his city from human need.
23. Socrates reaches theology only when the guardians must be educated.
24. Both Genesis and Plato's text read inner disorder on a larger scale.
25. Genesis moves from every imagination of the human heart to an earth filled with violence.
26. Socrates looks for justice written larger in a city.
27. When the respective readings break off, both the ark and the city are unfinished.
28. When the reading breaks off, the ark is waiting for its passengers.
29. When the reading breaks off, Socrates' city is waiting for its rulers.
